Linear peptides typically have several limitations as drug candidates:

1. Pharmacokinetic properties: Linear peptides often have poor bioavailability due to rapid degradation by proteases in the digestive tract and serum. They typically have short half-lives in circulation, poor membrane permeability, and are rapidly cleared by the kidneys. These are all pharmacokinetic issues (how the body processes the drug).

2. Pharmacodynamic properties: This relates to how the drug affects the body. While peptides can have high target specificity and potency, their pharmacodynamic properties are generally considered more favorable than their pharmacokinetic properties.

3. Synthesis: Modern solid-phase peptide synthesis methods have made peptide synthesis relatively straightforward, though there can be challenges with longer sequences.

4. Reagents: There is generally no shortage of suitable reagents for peptide synthesis in modern chemistry.

Based on my analysis, the major disadvantage of linear peptide scaffolds in chemical libraries for finding lead compounds is their poor pharmacokinetic properties - they are often unstable in biological systems, have poor oral bioavailability, and are rapidly cleared from the body. These issues make them challenging to develop into viable drugs despite potentially good activity in screening.
